tagline: Royal residences and temple sites line Kona’s coastal road
intro: Aliʻi Drive follows the Kailua waterfront past churches, markets, hotels and historic sites. Royal Footsteps Along the Kona Coast covers roughly seven miles of the road. Kailua Village Business Improvement District sponsored its nomination as the state’s second Hawaii Scenic Byway and presents it as a journey through seven centuries of royal archaeology, history and cultural traditions.

At Hōlualoa, a small beach trail became a wider highway in the nineteenth century, bisecting a royal complex. Road construction changed the Kailua shore again in the 1950s, when a seawall for Aliʻi Drive destroyed much of the beach at Kamakahonu. In 2013, the county council extended the Aliʻi Drive name south of Keauhou by renaming the adjoining Mamalahoa Bypass Road. Kamakahonu had been Kamehameha the Great’s residential compound from 1813 until his death in 1819. None of its houses or walls remain; the ʻAhuʻena heiau there was reconstructed in the 1970s.

Begin at Kailua Pier, where the oceanfront street starts. Kamakahonu lies beside the pier; Huliheʻe Palace stands on Aliʻi Drive. Continuing south, Hōlualoa Bay lies between Kailua-Kona and Keauhou Bay. Kahaluʻu Bay comes before Keauhou, where the historic shoreline includes Kamehameha III’s birthplace.

moments.title: Huliheʻe Palace
moments.text: Huliheʻe’s lava-rock construction acquired a new finish in 1885, when King Kalākaua had its exterior plastered. Governor John Adams Kuakini originally built the palace from lava rock. It later passed to Princess Ruth Keʻelikōlani, who made it her chief residence but preferred sleeping in a grass hut on the grounds. In 1927, the Daughters of Hawaiʻi, the Territory of Hawaii and custodian Stella Maude Jones worked together to restore the palace and turn it into a museum. Ruth invited reigning monarchs to vacation here, from Kamehameha III to Liliʻuokalani. The museum displays royal furniture and artifacts.

moments.title: Holualoa Bay
moments.text: Aliʻi Drive divides a royal complex that developed over centuries beside Hōlualoa Bay. Keākealaniwahine built a large complex here in the seventeenth century, in an area settled several hundred years earlier. Residential areas shared the complex with temples and burial areas. At Kamoa Point, additions included a terraced grandstand for watching surfing contests. The division came when the small beach trail was widened into a highway later in the nineteenth century. On the north side of the bay, a nineteenth-century Christian church was restored in the 1990s and is now known as Living Stones Church.

moments.title: Kahaluʻu Bay
moments.text: Two ancient fishponds, Waikuaʻala and Poʻo Hawaiʻi, remain visible at Kahaluʻu Bay. The bay was an important royal residence in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. At its north end, royalty used Kuʻemanu Heiau as a residence and a place to watch surfing. South of the bay, Hāpaialiʻi Heiau was built between 1411 and 1465 and restored in 2007. Surfers continue to use the bay, and green turtles are found in its waters. Across Aliʻi Drive stand the stone ruins of the original Helani Church, built in 1861. Its congregation uses a later church at a higher elevation.
